Notes

Sweet closes the mixtape by arguing with the drives that have kept it moving. The speaker values self-recognition over distant wealth, wants the struggle to end and immediately refuses to surrender first place. Attention compresses a life of effort into a thumb swipe; play is offered as protection against giving that contest everything. The defence of lonely people is emphatic but not the final resolution. Audience expectations and a wish for ignorance follow. The closer finds moments of self-acceptance without claiming that insight has removed the pressure to perform.

suǒ yǒu de lù dōu shì duì de

所有, every, leaves no wrong turn outside the opening verdict. Yet the song that follows is full of exhaustion, disappointment and self-questioning. The confidence therefore sounds retrospective: a route can have been worth taking without every moment on it having felt right. The closer begins with affirmation, then refuses to tidy up what that affirmation cost.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
yǎn guāng

眼光 is judgment, discernment or taste as well as an eye’s reach. The self-congratulation plants the visual vocabulary that will become magnifying glass, telescope and mirror. At first he praises his ability to choose; later the useful vision is the ability to see himself. The track gradually turns outward-looking taste toward self-recognition.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
shí xí jì zhě

A trainee reporter is a modest identity for someone who later claims the number-one place. It makes music a way of noticing and recording the surrounding world before it is a hierarchy to win. That fits the album's accumulation of daily objects, quoted speech and grotesque social scenes. Yet the reporter soon says he knows everything already. The tension between observation and exhausted certainty is present from the start.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
tào lù

套路 can be an established sequence, a formula or a manipulative routine. The next line’s repeated melodies brings the word directly into music, while “Ghost Dog” used it for distrusted social behavior. The recurrence connects two frustrations without making them identical: a predictable song and a predictable interaction can both feel as though the outcome has been arranged in advance.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
diàn tī

Immediately after rejecting shortcuts and reaching the summit in one step, the lyric puts people inside an elevator looking toward distant wealth. They have a mechanical route upward, yet the desired destination remains far away. The sigh punctures the fantasy of easy ascent. Movement and attainment are separated in a few ordinary objects.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
jīn shān yín shān

Gold and silver become entire mountains, giving wealth a size that overwhelms the people inside the elevator. The preceding 登顶, reaching a summit, makes the mountains both treasure and destination. This is aspiration rendered as landscape: something visible in the distance can structure a life’s motion while remaining out of reach.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
zhào yāo jìng

The revealing mirror is turned on the self, while the magnifying glass and telescope are declared less useful. The comparison changes the purpose of seeing: collecting more detail or reaching farther does not replace recognising one's own nature. Unlike the flawless reflection in 'Mirrors', this instrument is valuable because it can expose what a pleasing appearance conceals. The real blessing is not perfect innocence but a less flattering kind of access to oneself.

  • Ministry of Education dictionary: 照妖鏡
zhēn zhèng de fú qì

福气 names good fortune or the benefit of being blessed. The “real” version here is not first place or the gold-and-silver mountains: it is being able to recognize his own nature. “Mirrors” had good fortune shining beside a flawless reflection. The changed emphasis keeps the album’s language of blessing active while revising what counts as a fortunate outcome.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
yī tái dà jī qì

台 is the classifier for a machine, and 一台 makes the whole world one piece of equipment. The next complaint is that being himself is difficult because so many things affect him. The image supplies pressure and interdependence without explaining a complete system. It lets the lyric register being acted on before turning to the private war he fights inside that world.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
zì jǐ de zhàn zhēng

自己的 locates the conflict with the speaker, even though the previous lines describe forces acting on him from outside. The battle is not given a named enemy or a decisive victory. Its consequence is ongoing wear on mind and soul, followed by the unsettling claim to love the pain. The verse asks what sustained struggle does to the person who makes it habitual.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
shí jiān zhǔ yǔ

时间煮雨 is also the title of Yisa Yu’s 2013 song for the film Tiny Times. The exact phrase supplies a recognizable Mandopop echo here. Grammatically it makes time perform an impossible kitchen action, boiling rain, inside a reflection on two years of experience. The wording borrows an atmosphere of time passing without needing to reproduce or retell the other song.

  • Yisa Yu: 时间煮雨, Tiny Times film song
zhè dì yī shì wǒ de

The claim arrives immediately after wanting the torment to end. He is not simply announcing retirement from competition; the desire to win interrupts the wish to stop. This is central to the closer's honesty. The pressure is not only imposed by outsiders, because the speaker also wants the distinction the contest promises. Later advice to treat it as play has to contend with that investment rather than merely dismiss other people's demands.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
méi yǒu jìn tóu de guò shān chē

A roller coaster promises controlled ups and downs followed by an exit. Removing the end leaves the sensation without the reassurance that it is temporary. The preceding pairs move from anticipation to loss, excitement to numbness; the ride turns those emotional changes into a track laid out in advance. Repetition becomes tiring even when the peaks are real.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
dà mǔ zhǐ yī huà ér guò

The roller coaster gives the maker a long, exhausting sequence of expectation and disappointment. A single thumb movement then traverses it from the viewer's side. The unequal duration is the injury: what takes over one person's life can occupy only an instant of another's attention. The line helps explain why recognition never seems adequate to the effort spent pursuing it, without accusing every individual listener of deliberate cruelty.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
wán wán jiù hǎo le

The instruction to keep it playful echoes a recurring concern in Jackzebra’s catalog: his 2024 弓长张 EP includes 认真你就输了, whose title says taking it seriously means losing. Here the advice clashes with the refusal to surrender first place just earlier. Play is both a creative freedom and a defense against how much the contest already matters.

  • jackzebra: official discography, 弓长张 EP
méi bì yào pīn mìng

The key claim is that total exertion is not necessary. 'Ume' made that same life-staking effort the inevitable answer to being misunderstood; here the speaker withdraws the obligation. He can still care about music or rank while questioning whether either deserves the whole person. The force of the advice comes from the unresolved competitive refrain nearby: this is a limit being argued for from inside the attachment.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
míng chuí qīng shǐ

名垂青史 usually celebrates a name preserved in history. Adding 笑柄, a laughingstock, reverses the honor: lasting remembrance becomes lasting ridicule. This answers “Morning,” where dissolving into the river of history meant nobody would remember him. Across the two songs, being forgotten and being remembered wrongly become rival fears.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
gū dú de rén

The line reverses Zhang Chu's song title about lonely people being shameful, then eventually promotes them from not shameful to great. Repetition first removes a stigma and then supplies a counter-claim to worth. But the song continues into muttering, audience pressure and disappointment. The defence is a valuable position reached within the closer, not a magical resolution of its social isolation. Its insistence records how much defending is still needed.

  • Zhang Chu: 孤独的人是可耻的
wú yǔ

无语 commonly expresses exasperation, disbelief or having no adequate response, not literal loss of speech. It shares 语, “speech,” with the preceding 自语, talking to oneself. The paired words let him keep narrating while claiming to be beyond words. The song stages that contradiction rather than hiding it: speechlessness itself becomes another line to say.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
guān zhòng men de qī pàn

The audience's word is expectant hope, not an explicit threat. The next line names what that hope becomes for the performer: pressure that may be invisible to the people generating it. This broadens the album's earlier hostile-audience scenes. Even sympathetic attention can become a demand when somebody must repeatedly supply the version of themselves that others are waiting for. The burden does not require every listener to be an enemy.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
wú zhī

The final refuge contradicts both the opening claim to know everything and the earlier celebration of self-recognition. That contradiction should remain. The speaker has seen enough to want relief from seeing, yet cannot simply unlearn the experience the song has narrated. Repeating absolute belief in ignorance creates a wished-for shelter in language. The album ends with that effort to stop being burdened by knowledge, rather than a proof that the burden has gone.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
shēn xìn bù yí

深信不疑 is a firm idiom for profound, unquestioning belief. Its object is the claim that ignorance brings happiness, so the song ends with certainty about the value of not knowing. After self-examination and awareness of treacherous hearts, that conviction sounds like a refuge constructed in language. The repeated affirmation does not erase everything he has just shown us he knows.

About Jackzebra and this mixtape

Zhuang Zhuang Mixtape arrived on Surf Gang on October 2, 2026: 55 tracks, opening with Sour and closing with Sweet. Its cast widens from YoungQueenz on Poker Face to User116, Effie, kuru, yoyi, 春 and 南部犯罪份子. Aghast has a production credit on every track from Hitman through Snatch, giving that stretch a shared collaborator behind its changing scenes.

Surf Gang release · Artist credits

Jackzebra told AVYSS that he writes while singing over a beat he has listened to repeatedly, keeping the images in his head central. He values the room Mandarin leaves for indirect meanings. Listen for ordinary phrases becoming physical scenes: familiarity becomes cooking, authority becomes family seniority, and a tired saying suddenly turns into a threat.

AVYSS interview, 2024

In STATIC, he describes mixtapes as a format for letting ideas flow, reserving an official debut album for later. In a separate conversation about Above & Beyond, he compared that earlier tape to a collection of his producer friends’ work. The credits here likewise reward attention: long-running collaborators sit alongside guests working in Mandarin, Korean and English.

STATIC interview · Sabukaru interview, 2025

The small details connect to his stated interests: he has described playing Temple Run in transit and before shows, watching Top Boy, and wanting to score White Oleander. These give the songs specific points of contact with his life. The notes follow those connections alongside the lyrics’ jokes, invented scenes and competing voices.

His recommendations in Perfectly Imperfect · Dazed interview, 2025 · Interview questionnaire, 2025

Jackzebra has pushed back on being made to represent all of China’s underground. These notes stay close to the words: what an expression usually means, what changes in this line, and how another song answers it. Cultural references have sources; interpretations rest on details you can hear or read in the song.
